newValue: The alligator gar (Atractosteus spatula) is a living fossil from the lower Mississippi basin and Gulf Coast states of the south-eastern USA and northern/central Mexico - the largest exclusively freshwater fish in North America, essentially unchanged for roughly 100 million years. It occurs in large lakes, rivers, sluggish tributaries and backwaters, tolerates fresh and brackish water, and reaches a recorded 3.05 m with wild fish routinely aged past 50 years. Several US states restrict private possession, so check local regulations before acquiring one.

Provide floating cover over open water so the fish feels secure at the surface, and expect a jumper that will test any lid.

newValue: Obligate piscivore: whole prey items only - rotating tilapia, silversides/smelt, shell-on shrimp, squid and earthworms, with a weekly vitamin B1 supplement. Transition wild-caught fish onto frozen foods with the stick-and-jiggle method rather than live feeders.

newValue: Phractocephalus hemioliopterus is a giant long-whiskered catfish of the Amazon and Orinoco basins, inhabiting everything from rapids to flooded forest across much of northern South America. It is sold cheaply as a 5 cm juvenile, and Seriously Fish documents the consequences: public aquaria saturated with donated adults and feral populations established by dumped fish in the USA and several other countries. Both FishBase and specialist references treat it as an expert or public-aquarium species rather than a home-tank fish.

newValue: Gymnomuraena zebra is the sole member of its genus, a heavy-bodied, boldly banded moray with blunt molar-like teeth built for crushing shells. It is one of the widest-ranging morays on earth: FishBase records it across the Indo-West Pacific from the Red Sea and East Africa to the Society Islands, north to the Ryukyu and Hawaiian islands, south to the Great Barrier Reef, plus the eastern Pacific from southern Baja California to Colombia and the Galapagos, on reef-associated rocky and sandy bottoms from 3 to 50 m depth. newValue: The clown knifefish (Chitala chitala), also called the clown featherback, is a large Southeast/South Asian notopterid knifefish native to the Indus, Ganges-Brahmaputra and Mahanadi drainages, living in rivers, lakes, beels, reservoirs, canals and ponds. It reaches 122 cm and is listed as Near Threatened by IUCN. Caution on identity: aquarium literature routinely confuses C. chitala with C. ornata and C. lopis, and FishBase records from Thailand and Indo-China were actually C. ornata - so verify which fish you are buying, because care figures for the genus travel together.

Size the enclosure for the adult from day one, because a stunted 60 cm fish in a small tank is the failure mode, not the target.

newValue: Clown knives are nocturnal, territorial cave-dwellers: they spend the day in a chosen lair, backing in tail-first, and prowl the tank at night hunting largely by scent. Territoriality hardens with age - older fish are more sedentary and more territorial - and two knifefish in one tank will fight ferociously, so single housing is the default. Provide a definite cave each (or a very large tank with several options), subdued lighting, and expect activity bursts at feeding time rather than daytime display.

newValue: Carnivore and active predator: clown knives will eagerly swallow any fish that fits in their mouth, and wild fish eat aquatic insects, mollusks, shrimps and small fishes. Get them onto pellets and dry foods early (many resist), then vary with earthworms, bloodworm and other meaty items, fed after the lights go out to match their nocturnal rhythm. Remove uneaten food in the morning - leftover food is water quality damage on a fish that is already extremely sensitive to poor conditions - and never use feeder goldfish or livebearers as food.

It is a pelagic, open-water river fish that can live 20 years or more.

newValue: Iridescent sharks are peaceful but nervous open-water swimmers with poor eyesight: startled, they dash chaotically and injure themselves on glass, decor and tankmates, which is why crumpled tanks kill them. They are not aggressive - they are easily intimidated by boisterous fish and will eat anything small enough to swallow - and they constantly cruise the middle water column, bothering sedentary tankmates simply by being busy. Young fish school; adults become more solitary but still want their own kind, so plan for company and space together.

Feed small portions two to three times a day that are finished within 5-10 minutes, and do not let a greedy fish drive overfeeding - waste management is already the main maintenance load.

newValue: The longnose gar (Lepisosteus osseus) is a primitive, pike-like North American fish with a long, toothed snout and diamond-shaped ganoid scales, native from the St. Lawrence and Great Lakes through the Mississippi basin to the Gulf slope, and south into Mexico. It lives in sluggish pools, backwaters, oxbows and lakes, usually near vegetation, and occasionally enters brackish water. It is IUCN Least Concern and widespread, reaches 200 cm, and is an air-breathing fish whose eggs are poisonous - a legally regulated species in several US states even where it is native.

newValue: Longnose gars are sedentary ambush predators: they hang motionless near vegetation or float at the surface - where gulping air looks like basking - then explode forward in a sudden attack on passing fish. They are not documented as territorial aggressors; the real social problem is size, since anything not much larger than them is prey while larger active fish harass a sedentary gar in return. Expect a fish that uses the whole floor to turn, rests in open water rather than caves, and needs space to accelerate without hitting its snout.
